mappings.note: Retrieves what the book did -- opened butterfly migration to him. Extraction, not C-E2.2-LO-15, which is the science-fair defeat rather than the book.

The mother as a figure in the story: trips, equipment, challenges set. NOTE this frame has no outcome for her role at all -- LO-15 is the fair, LO-16 the scientist's own qualities -- so LO-4 (character) is the honest citation.
'What lesson does he learn when he wins nothing' is LO-15's first clause word for word.
'What experiments does he THEN undertake' is LO-15's second clause -- how the defeat changed his work. Not LO-1, because the 'then' is the whole point.
Asks for the qualities that make a scientist. The core LO-16 item.
Sets reading books against observing, thinking and experimenting -- the same list of qualities, generalised past Ebright. Not LO-15.
Asks the student to describe Ebright's DNA and cell work alongside their own science. Retrieval of what he did; no quality of a scientist is named, so not LO-16.

The stem itself says children's questions are the beginning of scientific inquiry, which is the curiosity quality LO-16 lists. No outcome in this frame covers answering the science questions themselves, and that gap is worth recording.
Invites the student's own questions -- curiosity practised rather than described. Same reasoning as the item before it.
Names Robert W. Peterson. Extraction.

Names the room-mate. Extraction. DEFECT: the key here is 'John', but another item in this same chapter is keyed 'James R. Wong' as the room-mate who drew his pictures and built his models. The two contradict; the text supports Wong.
Mr Weiherer. Extraction.
The working of DNA. Extraction.
Writing to Dr Urquhart for a real experiment is the action the defeat produced. Not LO-1: the significance is the change of method.
Monarchs are the ones birds avoid. Extraction.
Caterpillars. Extraction. NOTE the stem reads 'betties', which is an OCR corruption of 'beetles'; it appears in a second item in this chapter too.
Coins, rocks and butterflies. Extraction; the collecting habit as a quality is a different item.
Eighth grade. Extraction.
Twenty-five species. Extraction.
Butterflies. Extraction of the sentence's missing word.
Egg, caterpillar, pupa -- all named in the text. Extraction, although the content is biological.
Seventh grade is when the fair taught him what real science is. LO-15's moment, dated.
'The Travels of Monarch X'. Extraction.
Viceroy and monarch. Extraction.
The beetle experiment again, in MCQ form. Extraction.
Twenty-two. Extraction.
All three -- trips, telescopes and microscopes, encouragement -- build the mother as a character. Same treatment as the short-answer version.
The key is 'all of these': the grade, the fair, and the loss together. LO-15, not extraction, because the item asks what produced the insight.
Viceroys copy monarchs. Extraction.
The gold spots secreted a hormone. Extraction of his finding.
The theory of how cells work. Extraction.
The unknown hormone in the gold spots. Extraction.
Knowledge of monarch butterflies. Extraction.
Biochemistry and molecular biology. Extraction.

Realising that chasing butterflies one at a time could never yield enough is the first-rate mind LO-16 names -- seeing a better method. Not LO-1, because the insight rather than the fact is the answer.
Migration to Central America. Extraction.
He tagged monarchs. Extraction.
The National Academy of Science. Extraction.
It began with butterflies. Extraction.
Mapped as extraction of his ambition. DEFECT: the key is 'An astronomer', and the text says nothing of astronomy anywhere -- the supportable answer is option A, a scientist.
'The Travels of Monarch X' again, against near-miss titles. Extraction.
The University of Toronto. Extraction.

Retrieves his placings at the fair. Extraction. DEFECT of the known letter-versus-value kind: the item is keyed to option D while the model answer reads '(b) 1st and 2nd'. The VALUE '1st and 2nd' is option D's text, so the letter in the model answer is the wrong part.
Twelve gold spots. Extraction.
Cells grown from a monarch's wing. Extraction.
The chemical structure of the hormone. Extraction.
The cell-life theory as his most important discovery. Extraction.
James R. Wong drew the pictures and built the models. Extraction -- and the item that contradicts the 'John' key earlier in this chapter.
The social studies teacher. Extraction; Weiherer's opinion of HIM is a separate group of items.
Curiosity as the driver, illustrated from his life. LO-16's first named quality.
The mother's part in making him a scientist. LO-4 again for want of any outcome covering her; LO-16 would misattribute her encouragement to him as a quality.
Curiosity's importance, justified with examples -- exactly LO-16's 'illustrates each from his life'.
Weiherer's testimony is the text's source for the will to win for the right reasons, the third quality in LO-16.
The mother as companion, generalised to parents. LO-4, with the same gap noted: nothing in this frame carries her role.
Why the teacher valued the breadth of his interests -- the well-rounded character. Not LO-16, whose three qualities are all about scientific work.
The seventh-grade fair and its lesson, with both alternative phrasings pointing at the same thing. LO-15.
The book and its effect. Extraction; the change it caused is stated in the text rather than argued.
What makes him a winner, per Weiherer: wanting to do the best job rather than to take a prize. LO-16's will-to-win quality.
'Factors which contributed to making Ebright a scientist' is the qualities list, assembled. Not LO-15, which is one episode within it.
Two contributions, both stated in the text. Extraction.
Why he stopped tagging -- tedium and no feedback. Extraction.
Debating, canoeing, photography: the man beyond the laboratory. Character, not a quality of the scientist.
Names the book. Extraction.
Harvard, second in a class of 1,510, then Harvard Medical School. Extraction.
What the theory could lead to, as the text states it. Extraction.
'Four values which he projected' is the qualities list under another name. LO-16.
Viceroys copy monarchs because monarchs taste bad to birds. Extraction of his finding.
The X-ray photographs of the hormone's structure and the DNA conclusion. Extraction from the closing section.
'Science Is Real' is the fair's lesson as a title -- science is experiments, not display -- written as a blog post, which is the extended form LO-3 measures.
A talk show in the mother's voice, and what it reveals about her: character, at five marks. Not LO-16, which is about him.
A letter of thanks to the mother. Her role again, in the only outcome that can hold it, plus the long-answer form.
'Never stop questioning' is curiosity, justified from his life at five marks. Not LO-15: no defeat is involved.
A speech urging students towards science must set out what makes a scientist, which is LO-16, written at length.
'A well-rounded personality' is a character verdict covering debating, canoeing and photography as well as the science.
Two halves: the other interests (character) and Weiherer's opinion (the will to win). Both, at five marks.
The book's impact, assembled from the text into a long answer. Not LO-15: the book preceded the fair.
A diary entry about what his mother did for him. The mother again, as character, in extended written form.
Urquhart's contribution runs through the letter after the lost fair and the projects that followed, so it is LO-15's aftermath plus a second adult shaping him.
